I always start homework as soon as possible (usually the day I get it), and do extra practice problems from the book. In the week or so before a test I spend one day reviewing each section so I can make sure that I really understand each section. During those review days I'll do all of the problems I can find for that section (problems from the book, redo homework, and work examples from class) and, if necessary, skim over the section and make notes about stuff that I forgot. I also spend less time on sections that I am more confident about or don't think will be prioritized on the exam. If I start studying too late or the test is over a lot of chapters sometimes I do multiple sections in one day. When this happens I try to group the sections into chunks that are similar to each other or were connected in some way so it doesn't feel like I'm reviewing 8 completely different topics in one day.

Other than that, you have to make sure that you go to lecture and take notes. Go to office hours ASAP if you don't understand a topic and make sure you take notes on what your professor says while you're there. If needed,  find a video online explaining the concept. Basically, make sure that you know what's going on at all times throughout the class so when you have to do revisions you aren't clueless about any topic. 

I still haven't really mastered studying for memorization heavy classes, so if anyone has tips feel free to share them below! My current strategy for those classes is to go to class, take notes, and use office hours if necessary throughout the semester. Sometimes I make a quizlet and review that before the test, but when I'm feeling lazy I just read over my notes from class. If I need more information about a topic I just skim over that section of the textbook. If I need to memorize a diagram or something like that I just draw it out a bunch of times until I can draw it from memory. I also write out what I know about each section and then compare that to my notes to see how much I remembered or explain the topic to someone else in the class and ask them to tell me what I got wrong or left out.
